reason: Rich multi-source documentation confirms the rover's historic mission and its stunning 2010 laser rediscovery across six independent sites.
story: In November 1970, the Soviet Union soft-landed Luna 17 in the Moon's Sea of Rains, rolling out Lunokhod 1—the first remote-controlled rover on another world. Shaped like an eight-wheeled bathtub with a convex lid, it was designed to survive just three lunar days. Instead, powered by solar cells by day and warmed by a radioactive polonium core through freezing two-week nights, Lunokhod 1 survived eleven lunar days. Over nearly eleven months, it traversed over six miles, beamed back 20,000 television pictures, and probed hundreds of soil sites. Then, in the autumn of 1971, contact went silent. For almost four decades, the lost robot sat forgotten in the lunar dust. But in 2010, NASA orbiter photos pinpointed its coordinates. When physicists in New Mexico aimed a telescope laser at its French-built reflector, Lunokhod 1 fired back 2,000 photons on the very first try—blazing five times brighter than newer reflectors.
angle: Lost on the Moon for nearly 40 years, the world's first rover was pinged by an Earth laser in 2010 and bounced back 2,000 photons on the first shot—outshining every other retroreflector on the Moon.

claims.claim: Lunokhod 1 was the first remote-controlled robotic rover to land and operate on another celestial body.
The rover was transported to the Moon aboard the Luna 17 spacecraft, launched by the Soviet Union on November 10, 1970.
Luna 17 soft-landed in the Mare Imbrium (Sea of Rains) on November 17, 1970.
Lunokhod 1 rolled down dual ramps from the lander onto the lunar surface.
The vehicle consisted of a tub-like compartment with a large convex lid resting on eight independently powered wheels.
Lunokhod 1 carried a laser retroreflector supplied by France.
The rover used solar panels to recharge batteries during lunar day and a polonium-210 radioisotope heater to survive freezing lunar nights.
Designed for an operational lifetime of three lunar days, Lunokhod 1 exceeded expectations by operating for eleven lunar days.
The rover traveled a total distance exceeding 10 kilometers (over 6 miles) during its mission.
Lunokhod 1 transmitted approximately 20,000 television images back to Earth.
The rover conducted mechanical and soil density tests at approximately 500 lunar locations.
Operations officially ended in the autumn of 1971 after approximately 10 to 11 months of activity.
In March 2010, Albert Abdrakhimov located Lunokhod 1 and its lander on the Moon using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images.
On April 22, 2010, the APOLLO team at Apache Point Observatory successfully pinged Lunokhod 1's retroreflector with a 3.5-meter telescope laser.
Lunokhod 1 returned approximately 2,000 photons on the research team's first attempt after nearly 40 years of silence.
The return signal from Lunokhod 1 was surprisingly strong, outperforming the reflector on Lunokhod 2 by several times.

disputed: Soviet folklore alleged the rover was piloted by an internal dwarf; scripts should omit this or treat it purely as an urban legend.
Exact distance traversed varies slightly between 10.5 km, 10.54 km, and 'almost 7 miles'; scripts should safely phrase it as 'more than 6 miles' or 'over 10 kilometers'.
Mission operational span is variously stated as 321 Earth days, 322 Earth days, or 10 to 11 months; scripts should describe it as 'nearly 11 months' or attribute precise day counts.
